summary: Updates the rules for the special-use domain name ipv4only.arpa, which clients use to discover the NAT64 prefix of a network, as set out in RFC 7050. It is a standards-track document dealing with how this name is handled.

plainLanguage.summary: Some networks only speak the new Internet language and need a translator to reach older sites. A special name helps a device discover the translator, and this document sets the rules for that name.

questions: how do clients discover the nat64 prefix
why is ipv4only.arpa an insecure delegation
what does a dns64 resolver return for ipv4only.arpa
subtitle: Why the name ipv4only.arpa is officially special, and what resolvers and DNS64 servers must do with it.

tldr.problem: RFC 7050 uses the name ipv4only.arpa to let clients find their network's NAT64 prefix, but it said the name had no special properties, so software had no clear mandate to handle it specially.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC declares the special properties of ipv4only.arpa and its two reverse names. Client name resolution must send the query to the interface's own resolver, DNS64 resolvers must answer it themselves, and the zone must be an insecure delegation.
tldr.outcome: Software may now implement the special behavior legitimately, giving better performance, reliability and correctness. IANA recorded the names and the two IPv4 addresses.

today: RFC 8880 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 7050. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Omission This RFC Fixes
sections.content:
NAT64 (RFC 6146) lets IPv6 clients reach IPv4-only servers. DNS64 (RFC 6147) helps by synthesizing IPv6 addresses for IPv4-only servers, or by telling clients the network's NAT64 prefix so they can synthesize addresses themselves.

RFC 7050 defines the name ipv4only.arpa for discovering that prefix. But its Domain Name Reservation Considerations section said the name had no properties needing special handling, so it was never recorded in the Special-Use Domain Names registry.

Implementers were left to choose between skipping the special behavior the name needs or implementing it and being accused of not complying with IETF DNS specifications. This RFC removes that dilemma.
sections.plainLanguage: A special name was invented to help devices find a translator, but nobody wrote down that it was special. So programmers were not sure they were allowed to treat it specially.

sections.title: Why the Name Is Peculiar
sections.content:
No normal user looks up the IPv4 address of ipv4only.arpa. It is already known, from RFC 7050, to have exactly two IPv4 address records, 192.0.0.170 and 192.0.0.171, and no IPv6 records.

Yet clients often ask for its IPv6 AAAA records and expect positive answers. They are not learning from the name's real authoritative server. DNS is being used as an improvised client-to-middlebox protocol that asks a DNS64/NAT64 gateway to disclose the prefix it uses for IPv6 address synthesis.
sections.plainLanguage: Your device asks a question it already knows the real answer to. The point is not the answer but who replies: the translator on your own network.

sections.title: What Went Wrong Without It
sections.content:
For client libraries, the trouble starts when a device uses a recursive resolver other than the one it learned from the network, which is typically announced through IPv6 Router Advertisement options or DHCPv6. Users may configure a public resolver, and VPN software often diverts DNS to a company's private resolver. Neither can be expected to know the local NAT64 prefix. A device may have several NAT64 services at once, such as the local network and a corporate VPN, each possibly with a different prefix.

For DNS64 implementations, treating the name normally meant querying the authoritative arpa servers for answers already fixed by specification. That added load, and sometimes delay or failures, since those servers have at times been observed to be slow or unresponsive.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask the wrong helper, you get the wrong translator's address. And making helpers phone far-away offices for answers they already know just slows everything down.

sections.title: The New Special Rules
sections.content:
Name resolution APIs and libraries MUST recognize ipv4only.arpa as special. Queries for it and any subdomain MUST go to the recursive resolver learned for that specific network interface, regardless of manual DNS settings, VPN overrides or a local resolver on the loopback address. The NAT64 prefix is a per-interface property. On multihomed devices clients MUST use interface-aware name resolution APIs.

DNS64 recursive resolvers MUST recognize the name and its subdomains as special, MUST NOT query authoritative servers for it, and MUST act as authoritative for the zone. They MUST return 192.0.0.170 and 192.0.0.171 for A queries, synthesized records for AAAA queries, a no-error-no-answer response for other types except DS, and NXDOMAIN for every subdomain. Queries for DS are resolved the usual way.

Traditional forwarding resolvers SHOULD NOT treat the name specially, since they may sit downstream of a DNS64 resolver. Application software that meets the name in user input resolves it as usual. Authoritative servers and registrars need no special handling.

The reverse names 170.0.0.192.in-addr.arpa and 171.0.0.192.in-addr.arpa are also special. Each has one PTR record pointing to ipv4only.arpa. Applications SHOULD NOT treat them differently.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say: ask your own network's helper, not a far-off one. And a translator helper must answer right away from memory instead of calling anyone.

sections.title: DNSSEC and Security
sections.content:
DNS64 conflicts with DNSSEC, because a signed claim that a name has no AAAA records clashes with synthesized ones. The discovery mechanism lets a client learn the prefix, validate the signed IPv4 data itself and synthesize IPv6 addresses locally.

The ipv4only.arpa zone MUST be an insecure delegation. Answers to AAAA queries are made by the local DNS64 resolver, which has no signing key, so they could never validate. DNSSEC-capable resolvers MUST NOT try to validate those answers. This corrects RFC 7050, which had said the zone must be protected with DNSSEC.

Hardcoding the known A answers also lowers the risk of malicious devices on the path returning wrong answers. The RFC argues that a user-set resolver being overridden is not a real security issue, because this query is a middlebox protocol in disguise.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a wax seal proves an answer is real. Here the local translator writes the answer itself, so a seal would make it look fake. So this one name goes without a seal.

sections.title: IANA Actions
sections.content:
IANA created an insecure delegation for ipv4only.arpa and recorded three names in the Special-Use Domain Names registry: ipv4only.arpa., 170.0.0.192.in-addr.arpa. and 171.0.0.192.in-addr.arpa.. It also recorded 192.0.0.170 and 192.0.0.171 in the IANA IPv4 Special-Purpose Address Registry.

An appendix gives an example BIND 9 configuration showing how a DNS64 resolver can achieve the required behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: The official phone books now list the special name and its two special numbers.
